newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan refining margins hit from all sides.
newsitem.headline: Japan refining margins hit from all sides.

text.p: Things have gone from bad to worse for Japanese refiners, oil industry sources say.

Not only are middle distillate inventories at impressively high levels and fuel oil demand waning, but now, in the middle of the summer driving season, retail gasoline prices have hit their lowest level this decade, forcing wholesalers to absorb much of the loss.

The convergent forces have been especially bad news for refinery margins, where the profit reaped from processing a barrel of crude oil and selling the resultant products has fallen below $1.00 per barrel in most cases and below zero in some, oil industry sources said.
"Refiners in Japan are very confused at this point," said one crude trader with a Japanese refiner.
"Their normal countermeasures against poor margins are just not available at present," he said.

With Japan's average retail gasoline prices falling below a break-even level of 103 yen a litre as of July 14 because of continuing fierce competition among retailers, wholesalers have been forced to protect many of their retail outlets from bankruptcy by buffering the cost of products and swallowing the loss within their own refining margin.

"In theory, refining margins in Japan should be constant, as wholesale prices are set to reflect crude prices, but the theory breaks down when retailers are in such bad shape," said a manager with another Japanese refiner.
"In many cases we are having to subsidise our wholesale price in order to allow our dealers to survive," he said.
Pump prices in major cities have fallen to 90 yen per litre and below, compared to last summer's levels of 100 to 110 yen.
Refiners also said the typical countermeasure of purchasing crude grades with a lower gasoline yield is no longer an option because of the resultant high yield of fuel oil.

Fuel oil buying by power utilities dropped some 12 percent in the first five months of this year from the same period in 1996, mainly because of growing use of nuclear power and liquefied natural gas in electricity generation.
"Crude grades with lower gasoline yields tend to have a much higher fuel oil yield, so with both markets doing poorly, we get burned either way," said a crude trader with a leading refiner.

For example, Indonesian Duri, commonly used for direct burning by utilities in Japan, can also be used for its low, two percent topping yield of gasoline. But the resultant fuel oil yield is as high as 79 percent, an unwelcome outcome in a soft fuel oil market.
"And utilising our secondary refining units to reprocess the fuel oil simply creates more middle distillate, which we do not need," the trader at the leading refiner said.
Latest data shows Japan kerosene stocks up some 47 percent over year-earlier levels and gas oil stocks up 9.6 percent from a year earlier.
Crude traders said the relative strength of the yen versus the dollar in recent weeks, which makes imports of crude cheaper in yen-terms, had offered the only support for withering margins.
